title: Death by day and night
hookLine: sunset photos land because the light is leaving; the Buddha chose that hour for remembering (AN 6.20)
tomorrow: no one escapes it. so why do we act like we might?

lines: YOU CAN WATCH A DAY END.
cards: Sunset is the hour people post: the orange sky, the silhouette, the caption. Part of why it lands is that the light is visibly leaving. You can watch a day end.
The Buddha used exactly that hour. When the day is gone and night comes on, he told his monks, the bhikkhus, sit with a question. And again when night is gone and day comes on.

teach.h: MANY THINGS COULD BRING MY DEATH.
teach.b: The sutta is short, in the Anguttara Nikaya, right after yesterday's. At the day's end, reflect: many things could bring my death tonight.
A snake, a scorpion, a stumble in the dark, a meal that turns against me, a sickness stirring in the body. Then comes the real question.
Is there anything unskillful in me I haven't let go of, a grudge, a craving, a lie, that would stand in my way if I died tonight?

teach.h: IF SO, LIKE A TURBAN ON FIRE.
teach.b: If there is, the Buddha says, put everything into letting it go, the way someone whose turban had caught fire would put everything into putting it out. And if there isn't?
Then live in joy and gladness, and keep training, day and night. That second answer is easy to miss. The reflection isn't only alarm.
It ends in gladness for anyone who checks and finds nothing left undone. Then the whole thing again at dawn: if I die today. Why these two hours?
The sutta doesn't explain. But the senses make the case on their own. At dusk the light drains out of the room and the body feels it.
At dawn it comes back, and nobody earned it. Two times a day, the sky itself says: this doesn't last.

how: Some Buddhists fold the AN 6.20 reflection into their evening and morning chanting or sitting; in Theravada monasteries the recollection of death is often among the short reflections recited in daily chanting.

games.q: what does “death by day and night” mean?
o: remembering death at the day's end and the night's end
a festival held for the dead at sunrise and sunset
a monk's fast from dawn until dusk each day

games.q: the dusk reflection — tap the pairs.
p: like a turban on fire: put it out

s: the dusk reflection is meant only to make you afraid
for anyone who checks and finds nothing left undone, the sutta ends in joy and gladness.
the Buddha uses the image of a turban on fire for urgent effort
if something unskillful remains, put everything into letting it go, like putting out a burning turban.
the sutta explains exactly why dusk and dawn were chosen
it doesn't say. the senses make the case: light leaving, light returning.

games.q: it's late and you're scrolling. you remember the dusk question, and a fight with your brother is still sitting there, unrepaired. what does the sutta point you to?
o: put real effort into letting the grudge go, like putting out a fire.
nothing tonight; death reflection is for monks in monasteries.
feel guilty about it until you fall asleep, as a reminder.
games.why: if something unskillful remains, the Buddha says to put everything into letting it go. guilt isn't the practice; letting go is.

practice: Turn toward the nearest window or lamp and look at the light itself: its color, where it falls, where it fades. Ask the sutta's question once, gently: if this were my last evening, is anything left unforgiven?
If something comes, note it; if nothing does, let the other answer in, gladness.

wordCard.voice: Death by day and night: the reflection at dusk and at dawn, ending either in effort or in gladness.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: death, dying; the first half of maranassati, mindfulness of death.

carryVoice: Keep this one close: dusk and dawn, the two hours that remember for you. Day sixteen twenty-eight, at dusk.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.20 (Maranassati Sutta, second: reflecting when day departs and night arrives, and when night departs and day arrives; the causes of death; the turban-on-fire simile; joy for one who finds nothing unabandoned)
